newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan cabinet mulls IMF package, markets wait.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan cabinet mulls IMF package, markets wait.

text.p: Pakistani Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto held a cabinet meeting on Sunday to discuss an economic rescue package already submitted to the International Monetary Fund for approval, government sources said.
They said the new measures, expected to slash spending and impose an agricultural income tax, were likely to be announced after the cabinet meeting, which began at 10 a.m. (0500 GMT).
At the Karachi Stock Exchange, dealers waited nervously for details of the package, but the index moved up 7.86 points or 0.58 percent to 1,364.15 at noon on short-covering.

"Major players want to wait and see what the new measures are and what would be the IMF reaction," analyst Nauman Sheikh of KASB & Co said. "There is still uncertainty about the fate of the standby facility and conflicting news about what the government has really agreed to in its talks with the IMF."
Pakistan, faced with a yawning current account deficit and shrinking foreign reserves, is under IMF pressure to reduce its budget deficit to four percent of gross domestic product.
Pakistani newspapers have quoted official sources as saying the fiscal deficit in 1995/96 stood at 5.8 percent, but the government has not announced an exact figure.
Bhutto's economic adviser Shahid Hasan Khan, who led the Pakistani team in last week's talks with the IMF in Washington, returned to Islamabad on Sunday to join the cabinet meeting.

The official news agency APP said an IMF mission would arrive in Pakistan on Thursday for a review of the economy which must be completed before the fund releases further tranches of a stalled $600 million standby loan.
The IMF withheld disbursements due in June and September because of dissatisfaction with Pakistan's economic policies and confusion surrounding the fiscal 1996/97 (July-June) budget.
"An agreement has been reached between the Pakistan delegation and management of the IMF on stabilisation and reform policies," said a joint communique after the Washington talks.
It made clear that the IMF, disappointed by failures to implement agreed policies, would accept nothing on trust.
"Implementation of prior actions and agreement on the letter of intent would pave the way for the Fund management to present to its board the programme for approval," the statement said.
The IMF provided the standby loan in December after Pakistan staved off a foreign exchange crisis by devaluing the rupee seven percent against the dollar and imposing new taxes.

The package failed to turn the economy around or plug the budget gap, forcing Bhutto's economic managers to draft another tax-heavy budget that aroused a wave of confidence-eroding strikes and opposition protests after it was unveiled in June.
The government made tax concessions to placate various interest groups, but alienated the IMF in the process.
Sameer Ahmed, head of sales at ING Baring Securities, said the future direction of the Karachi bourse depended on what measures the government had to implement to satisfy the IMF.
"I don't see any major buying coming into the market right now. The package may itself infuse negative sentiment," he said.
